en: General Exposition of the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* Compiled by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Xuanzang;
Expounded by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Huan, Ming Dynasty.
Regarding the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* (*Ba shi gui ju*):

Initially, after Dharma Master Xuanzang had completed his compilation of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Dharma Master Kuiji, seeing that the ten fascicles of the root treatise were voluminous in text and profound in meaning, requested that the Master collect these essential points.
The eight consciousnesses are divided into four chapters, with each chapter consisting of twelve verses.

The fifty-one mental associates (*caitta*) are each assigned to their respective positions within the fundamental consciousnesses, differing in number according to their specific functions; thus, they are arranged in a systematic and orderly fashion, which is why it is called a "rule" (*niyama*).
Although the treatise consists of ten fascicles, its essential meaning is fully contained within these forty-eight lines, encompassing everything without exception.
This legacy may be called the most concise and essential; it serves as the key to the entire Great Canon of Teachings.

Not only do lecturers fail to understand it and thus find it difficult to penetrate the framework of the teachings, but even practitioners of Chan meditation, if they do not understand this, will remain ignorant of the number of times their own minds arise and cease.
It is truly the very essence of the Buddha-dharma. However, regarding Master Kuiji’s traditional commentary:

The commentaries on these treatises are difficult for students to clarify; consequently, they merely cling to superficial characteristics and are unable to harmonize them with the fundamental principle of "Mind-Only.

While I was residing at Jizhao on Mount Shuangjing, I happened to receive the request of Master Kai of Danju to inquire further into the principles of the two schools of Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang).
Undaunted by my own meager learning, I first relied upon the *Awakening of Faith* to synthesize the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, and subsequently, based on the meanings of the treatises, [I proceeded to...]
The prose of this work is condensed into verse so that students may grasp its meaning at a single glance and see it clearly.
Thus, practitioners of Chan need not extensively study the doctrinal teachings; they can verify and seal their minds through this very text.

By means of this, they may gauge the depth of their realization and awakening, and even in their daily activities of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they will be able to discern the arising and ceasing of mental states.
However, there are already many recent commentaries on this verse that have all captured its essential meaning.

Nevertheless, as it may serve as an aid depending on the specific capacity of the practitioner, and because the text is difficult to clarify word by word, I have first presented the general outline above so that one may understand the core principles;
thus, regarding the verses themselves, one need not labor over a detailed exegesis, for they will be easily understood.
The general outline is as follows: The one true *dharmadhātu*, the perfectly luminous and wondrous mind, is fundamentally devoid of even a single thing and is entirely without body or mind.
Since the characteristics of worlds do not exist, how could there be the dualistic opposition of sense organs and objects, or the reflected images of deluded conceptualization?

Examining this mind and its objects, they all arise because of ignorance and non-awakening; one becomes consciousness by being deluded regarding the One Mind. This is the teaching of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Transformation gives rise to the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the appearance-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Therefore, the seeing-part is the mind and the appearance-part is the object.

Thus, those who discriminate between beauty and ugliness or engage in acceptance and rejection based on objects are merely deluded consciousnesses. If one realizes that mind and objects are but consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), then such discrimination will not arise.
When discrimination does not arise, the single mind is perfectly luminous and forever free from all marks.

Since one has not yet awakened to this single mind, it is necessary first to understand that the mind and its objects are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Thus, the arising and ceasing of mental activities will immediately vanish, and one can enter the single mind.
Therefore, regarding *vijñaptimātra*, one must first know the general outline before one can settle the mind and enter contemplation.
This verse outlines the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings (*citta-rāja*). When they take objects as their conditions, those objects may be pleasant or unpleasant;

consequently, the mental factors (*caitta*) follow them by grasping at these qualities, giving rise to aversion and attraction, or acceptance and rejection. Thus, one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds.

With these wholesome and unwholesome acts as causes, the two retributions of suffering and happiness are experienced. Therefore, through the drawing power of karma, sentient beings undergo suffering and pleasure.

Such is the nature of death; it is nothing more than this. Within this, the variations in the number and types of mental factors (*caitta*) associated with each of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), as well as the differences in the strength of the karma they produce, are clearly set forth.

This allows the student to investigate the mind thoroughly, to understand the point of origin and cessation of mental states, and to facilitate their cultivation and regulation, thereby avoiding blind practice and aimless training. It is not... [end of fragment].
They merely know the names and characteristics [of phenomena]. In the daily activities of sentient beings—seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—they do not depart from mind and objects.

This cognizing mind possesses three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Valid cognition" means the act of measuring; it excludes true wisdom. Now, when deluded consciousness confronts an object, there is immediately an act of measurement;
thus, the mind has three types of valid cognition: direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
The first moment of cognition appears clearly before one, without giving rise to discrimination, without being accompanied by verbal designations, and without a mind of deliberation;

this is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If, at the same time, the sudden mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) follows what is seen and immediately discriminates it, this is called inference (*anumāna*).
When one engages in conceptual estimation without [direct] naming, this is called non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). These three types of valid cognition are capable of...

This refers to the mind that takes an object as its condition (*ālambana*). Furthermore, there are three types of objects so conditioned: the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), the realm with a shared substance (*sābhāsa-viṣaya*), and the realm of solitary images (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) takes the objective realm as its condition. "Objective" (*svabhāva*) means real. This refers to the actual dharmas of the sense faculties and their objects, which are fundamentally the wondrous nature of *tathatā* (suchness).
Being neither beautiful nor foul, because the mind is free from discrimination, the object likewise lacks beauty or foulness. This is [the first type].

Regarding the nature of objects (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) and objects with substantiality (*sadravya-viṣaya*): these are the objects of inference (*anumāna*). If one’s inferential estimation does not correspond [to reality], it is considered non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
These objects with substantiality are either real or similar, because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses each have their own respective objects.
If the six consciousnesses externally perceive the five sense-objects and infer characteristics such as long or short, square or round, beautiful or ugly, this belongs to the second category.

Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) engages in conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it constitutes inference (*anumāna*). These characteristics such as length and so forth arise by bearing the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that external object;
thus they are called "resembling the bearing of an essential nature" (*sadṛśasvabhāvābhāsa*).

Because this is provisional (*prajñapti*), when the mental consciousness takes as its object the past shadows of the five sense-objects that have already fallen away, it is also called "having an essential nature and being a solitary shadow" (*sasvabhāva-kevalābhāsa*). Since these are transformations produced by the mental consciousness, it is said: "By means of..."

When the mind takes form as its object, it appears as if possessing a substantial basis; in this case, a portion of the mental aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises at one end of the process, because it arises solely from the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the subjective faculty of cognition.
If the mind takes objects such as empty flowers or the horns of a rabbit as its focus, these are termed "solitary images without a substantial basis.
Furthermore, objects perceived by a distracted mind, as well as those within dreams or seen during the delusions of illness, are all considered non-valid cognitions (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, phenomena such as the fish, rice, and mountains of meat that appear within meditative concentration are all direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*).

Although the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) may pertain to all three types of valid cognition, it is predominantly direct perception and only rarely inferential. If the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its self, the intermediate image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises at both ends;
because the subject and object are identical in being transformations of the same seeing-part, this is called "truly carrying" (*saha-nīta*).
The substantial object: this is the distinction between the mind and its objects.

When the mind and its objects are confronted, if the objects possess opposition or conformity, beauty or ugliness, then the perceiving mind arises in dependence upon them, giving rise to views such as hatred and love, or acceptance and rejection. Thus, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma.

Tainted by these [afflictions], they become of two natures, good and evil; thus, they bring about the two retributions of suffering and pleasure in the future. Consequently, the mind-king experiences the feelings of suffering and pleasure.
If neither good nor evil arises, it belongs to the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), and there is then a neutral feeling.
Because of this, feelings are also threefold. For this reason, sentient beings in the three realms ascend and descend, floating and sinking, revolving through suffering and pleasure.
Forgetfulness arises entirely from the internal habit-energies of consciousness-only transforming and giving rise to the mind and its objects.

Therefore, the three means of valid cognition, the three objects, the three natures, and the three feelings—through these, one cannot escape birth and death; all are the fault of the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Sentient beings revolve in dependence upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Now, in the school of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*), because ordinary people do not realize during their daily activities that suffering and pleasure have no creator and no experiencer, non-Buddhists falsely posit a "divine self" (*ātman*), and those of the Two Vehicles grasp at phenomena as existing outside the mind.
Thus, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are consciousness-only, so that by knowing they are consciousness-only, one knows they do not transcend one's own mind.

Because the mind does not see the mind, there are no characteristics to be apprehended. Therefore, when practicing Chan meditation and applying effort, one is taught to investigate apart from the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and to seek apart from the realm of deluded thoughts.
This is precisely to lead people directly to their own minds, where fundamentally no such thing exists.
Now, the fact that the Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses are called "rules" (jǔgǔ) is merely to clarify the nature of the mind and its objects. Its...
Whether the deeds performed are wholesome or unwholesome, they are all brought to completion through the assistance of the mental factors (*caitta*).

Because these factors vary in their degree of presence—some being more numerous and others fewer—their power is correspondingly unequal, being either strong or weak. This is the general outline of the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).

As for the mental factors themselves, they have already been presented among the "One Hundred Dharmas. Here, I shall list them in advance along with their corresponding objects; thus, there will be no need for further detailed explanation when we encounter the actual texts, lest it hinder the flow of the discussion.

Observe the mind alone. In the practice of Zen, if one realizes that both the deluded mind and deluded objects are merely manifestations of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), then at the time of applying effort, one should simultaneously let go of both internal faculties and external objects.

Without pursuing the shadows of conditions, and with both subject and object forgotten, free from all duality, one simply upholds a single thought-moment and gathers it back into one’s own mind. Thus, all objective measures and conceptual discriminations are...
This is the remainder of the dharma.
The five consciousnesses have real objects as their nature and are direct perception; they pervade all three moral natures. The three—eye, ear, and body—reside in two stages.
The universal, the specific, the eleven wholesome, the two intermediate, the eight great, and greed, anger, and delusion—this verse refers to the first five consciousnesses.
The first line states that the five consciousnesses share the same substance as the eighth consciousness.

When they perceive objects, they belong exclusively to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the first five consciousnesses are the refined essence of the eighth consciousness reflected within the gates of the five sense organs.
This refers to the function of directly apprehending an object. When the sense organ first reflects the object, at the very first moment of cognition, no conceptual discrimination has yet arisen;
it is devoid of linguistic designations and lacks any deliberative mind. Therefore, this is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The object is a "real object" (*dharmatā-viṣaya*).

If a second moment of conceptual discrimination arises, then—whether functioning simultaneously with the mental consciousness or arising in association with it—it belongs to inference (*anumāna*). Thus...
It is said that the nature of the object is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding the "three natures," these refer to the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Because the essence of these five consciousnesses is neither constant nor investigative, they all pertain to the three natures. Question: Since the five consciousnesses are direct perceptions and inherently lack wholesomeness or unwholesomeness, why do they pertain to all three natures?
Answer: This refers to the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which induces its own kind [of seeds].

If the seeds arise simultaneously, then all three natures are applicable; this refers to the spontaneous functioning of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), not exclusively to the five sensory consciousnesses.

Question: If the preceding [consciousness] is of the same substance as the eighth, and yet the eighth consciousness is ultimately neither wholesome nor unwholesome, why is it that the five consciousnesses alone are said to be applicable to all three natures? Answer: The eighth consciousness never gives rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

The five consciousnesses possess spontaneous discrimination (*svarasa-vikalpa*); this is said to be "pervasive" (*sāmānya*) with respect to their function during the subsequent stage of discrimination.
Regarding the statement that the three—eye, ear, and body—dwell in two stages: this refers to the grounds where the five consciousnesses of the three realms operate and cease. These two stages are:
the Stage of Mixed Dwelling in the Five Destinies of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the Stage of Joy Born of Seclusion in the First Dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). This is because...
The five consciousnesses of the desire realm are fully present. The beings of the first dhyāna heaven take the joy of meditation as their food;

because they do not consume solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), they are devoid of the tongue-consciousness. Since they do not receive food, they likewise do not perceive odors; thus, they lack the nose-consciousness.
They possess only the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body. "Dwelling" means to abide; it signifies that these three consciousnesses also abide in the first dhyāna.

Dhyāna. If one reaches the second dhyāna, which is the stage where joy and bliss arise, because the three consciousnesses [of the eye, ear, and nose] are also absent within that meditative absorption, it is said that they "dwell" therein.
The two phrases concerning "universal" (sarvatraga) refer to the associated mental factors (caitta).
These associated mental factors generally number fifty-one; however, the first five consciousnesses possess only thirty-four such mental factors. The remainder...
That which is incomplete is so because the factors are mutually contradictory.
The five consciousnesses rely upon the same pure material sense organs (*rūpa-indriya*). The nine conditions attend to the seven; the eight and seven are adjacent and conjoined.
Three are separated from two as they contemplate the world of objects. For the ignorant, it is difficult to distinguish between consciousness and the sense organs.
The first phrase of this verse refers to the sense organs that serve as the supports for the five consciousnesses. The second phrase refers to the conditions for the arising of these consciousnesses.

The third phrase refers to their function of cognizing objects. Regarding "relying on the organs," it means that the essence of the eight consciousnesses, which is luminous and subtle, now reflects at the gates of the five organs, each cognizing its own respective object.
The reason they cannot achieve universal penetration (*yuan-tong*) is because they are obstructed by the five material organs.
Because they are so enshrouded, they are each distinguished separately. Now, the five sense organs are produced from the four great elements;

there are both the superficial (the *tuccha-mūla*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Here, the pure material organ (*viśuddha-rūpa-indriya*) is produced from the purified four great elements and constitutes the ultimate organ;
thus, the superficial organ is not to be relied upon. Furthermore, consider one who is blind seeing darkness: it is no different from having eyes while being in the dark.

This is different. It is clear enough that while the faculty of the feet is destroyed, the faculty of sight is not; thus, that which serves as the support must be the pure material faculty (*rūpa-prasāda*).

Regarding what is called "pure material," the ancient interpretation merely states it is the pure matter formed at the initial creation of the four great elements. This is most difficult to understand, for it can only be seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
I, the ignorant one, maintain that this "pure matter" is none other than the shell of ignorance (*avidyā-kośa*). How is this known? Consider, for instance, the wondrous clarity...
The true mind is fundamentally perfect, luminous, and vast. Now, having transformed into consciousness, it is constrained and obstructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).

When it combines with form to constitute the sense organs, the essence of the ignorant consciousness takes up residence within them; this constitutes the sentient being of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Furthermore, were it not for the power of ignorance, who could wrap this wondrous mind and cause it to enter the physical shell?
Is it not so? Therefore, the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) also possesses a physical form; it is merely subtle and light.

That ghosts and spirits possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) is sufficient evidence for this, as these are functions of pure matter (*rūpa*). Regarding the "nine conditions" and so forth, this refers to the conditions for the arising of consciousness;
that is, there are nine conditions for the emergence of the eight consciousnesses, differing only in the number of conditions they require. As for the nine conditions:

These are: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), clarity (*prakāśa*), faculty (*indriya*), object (*viṣaya*), attention (*manasikāra*), discrimination (*vikalpa*), defilement and purity (*saṃkleśavyavadāna*), seeds (*bīja*), and the fundamental [consciousness] (*mūla*).

These nine universally serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness, for conditioned phenomena do not arise without conditions. The verse says: Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions; Ear-consciousness arises from only eight;

Nose, tongue, and body [consciousnesses] from seven, three, and seven [respectively]; The latter three [mental consciousnesses] from five, three, four, and three [respectively]. This refers to the eye...
Consciousness necessarily arises by depending on nine conditions. Ear-consciousness depends on eight conditions, excluding the condition of light, because one can hear in the dark.
The three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body exclude both the conditions of light and space; therefore, they depend on only seven. This refers to their sequential order;

it should rather be stated as "eight and seven. As for the subsequent mental consciousness, it depends on five conditions, namely, excluding the conditions of discrimination and the sense organ, because the organ...

This is because the seventh consciousness is the basis for defilement and purity. Regarding the three conditions for the seventh consciousness: there are only attention (*manasikāra*), seeds, and the fundamental [consciousness].
Regarding the four conditions for the eighth consciousness: these are the faculty (*indriya*), namely the *manas*; the object (*viṣaya*), namely the seeds, the body-faculty, and the receptacle-world;
attention, which is one of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*); and seeds, which are the direct generative seeds of the eight consciousnesses. This is a general explanation.
Regarding the conditions for the arising of consciousness: "intention" (*manas*) refers to the first five consciousnesses; by extension, it also includes the final three.

The nose, tongue, and body apprehend objects through contact, because they only know them when in contact. The eye and ear apprehend objects without contacting them, because contact would destroy the sense organ.
This speaks to the function of clearly perceiving objects. The phrase "the fool finds it difficult to distinguish" refers to those of the Hīnayāna.
You establish the roots of defilement and purity based solely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, yet you do not understand the eight consciousnesses and their three divisions.

This is because the sense organs (*indriya*) are matter (*rūpa-dharma*) belonging to the objective division (*nimitta-bhāga*), whereas consciousness (*vijñāna*) is mind belonging to the subjective division (*darśana-bhāga*). Failing to understand this, you merely claim that the organ and consciousness arise from one another.
Even if we grant that the five consciousnesses arise in dependence upon the five organs, then upon what would the sixth consciousness depend as its organ?
The Sūtra states: "The faculties can illuminate objects, and consciousness can discern them; because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this, they are called fools.
The first eight lines of this verse praise impure consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*); the final four lines praise the attainment of wisdom (*jñāna*) which is free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Transforming appearances and contemplating emptiness occur only through the subsequently attained wisdom; even within the fruition, it still does not fully express the ultimate truth.
Perfectly luminous, its initial arising constitutes the outflow-free state; the three types of emanation bodies bring rest to the wheel of suffering.

These four lines praise the transformation of consciousness into wisdom. "Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) means to manifest or carry forth; "appearances" (*nimitta*) refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). By means of the five... [text fragment ends]

Consciousness invariably takes the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the five sensory objects as its condition. Because this consciousness functions simultaneously with the eight [consciousnesses], it now relies upon their objective aspects and transforms them into the contemplation of emptiness;
only then does it become wisdom. Although these aspects are empty, they have not yet transcended the characteristic of emptiness.
Because one cannot directly perceive the principle of the signless *tathatā*, wisdom is divided into fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).

Fundamental wisdom takes *tathatā* as its object and is called "true wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*); subsequently attained wisdom takes the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as its object and is called "provisional wisdom" (*prajñaptijñāna*).

The statement that "the fruit does not describe the true" precisely means that even within the stage of the Buddha-fruit, it is still termed provisional wisdom. This refutes the calculations of heterodox masters. Because...

The school of Master Sthiramati asserts that the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) takes suchness as its object within the causal stage; therefore, this [text] refutes that view. Regarding "the perfect luminosity first arises":

this refers to the transformation of the eight consciousnesses into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). At the moment it first arises, these first five consciousnesses immediately become untainted (*anāsrava*), because they share the same essence.
This is what is meant by the statement: "The fruit of the fifth and eighth is perfected. If these five [consciousnesses] transform into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*)...

When wisdom resides within the fruit of Buddhahood, it is able to manifest three types of bodies: namely, the great transformation body (*mahā-nirmāṇa-kāya*), the small transformation body, and the transformation body that accords with various classes of beings.

By means of these three bodies, one responds to the capacities of sentient beings and benefits them. Because there was external activity while on the path of causes, the great function of benefiting living beings is likewise accomplished upon the attainment of the fruit.

When ignorance is shattered through Zen meditation, then at the gates of the five sense faculties, all— (Note: The source text appears to be truncated; the translation provided reflects the full extent of the available text.)

The illumination of the wisdom of radiance is like a mirror reflecting objects: it neither welcomes nor rejects, responding to conditions all day long without a single dharma ever confronting the mind.
○ Verse on the Six Consciousnesses:
The three natures and the three means of valid cognition pervade the three objects; when the wheel of the three realms turns, they are easily known.
The associated mental factors number fifty-one; good and evil are assigned accordingly as circumstances arise. This verse concerns the six consciousnesses.
The first line states that the six consciousnesses possess the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. [They also involve] direct perception and inference.

It is not a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). It possesses all three types of objects—those with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), those with a substrate (*sanimitta*), and those that are mere mental images (*pratibimba*)—each of which it fully contains.

Since among all the consciousnesses only this one is complete in these respects, its power is the strongest. The birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) of the three realms, along with the causes and effects of good and evil, are created solely by this consciousness;
therefore, it is said that "the turning of the wheel of the three realms is easily known. The reason it is able to grasp the birth-and-death of the three realms is due to the five... [factors].
The eleven mental factors (caitta-dharma) are fully present; therefore, the power of karma is particularly eminent.

However, when a single thought-moment of either good or evil arises, the mental factors assemble together, following their respective categories. Thus, it is said that by classifying and assigning them accordingly, they become easy to understand.
Nevertheless, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) has five distinct ways of perceiving objects. These five modes are: the clear and distinct [consciousness]...

Regarding consciousness: there are five types of objects perceived by the five kinds of independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—namely, the independent mental consciousness in the state of non-concentration, the independent mental consciousness in meditative absorption, the independent mental consciousness in dreams, and the independent mental consciousness in a state of distraction.
Among these five, only the latter two—the states of dreaming and distraction—perceive exclusively "solitary shadows" (*kevala-pratibimba*).
The former three are all capable of perceiving all three types of objects, because wherever there is a shadow, [it is necessarily accompanied by a substance].
All such [notions] fall into the mold of mental consciousness; therefore, the practice of Chan meditation must necessarily transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness.
This is so that one does not fall into the gateway of shadows and reflections, for these are not the ultimate reality.
The natures, elements, and sensations constantly shift and change; The faculties follow faith and the rest, being generally interconnected;
Movement of the body and the utterance of speech are preeminent alone; Attraction and fulfillment are drawn by the power of karma.
This verse [shows] that the power of karma is strongest among the six consciousnesses. Although "sensation" is said to be threefold, in reality there are five. Internally...
The external [objects] differ in being coarse or subtle; these are termed suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity (*upekṣā*). That which oppresses or delights the mind is called grief or joy;
that which oppresses or delights the body is called suffering or pleasure. When grief, joy, suffering, and pleasure are not active, it is termed the feeling of equanimity.
Thus, these six consciousnesses are constantly transforming and shifting through the three natures, the three realms, and the five feelings. It is just as when one is virtuous...
Suddenly a single evil thought arises; when there is joy, suddenly a single sorrowful thought arises. They change and are unstable. The following sentence takes this up:
"When an evil thought arises, it arises in conjunction with the root [afflictions] and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
when a wholesome thought arises, wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) likewise arise in conjunction. This is because of these wholesome and unwholesome mental concomitants (*caitta*).

They function simultaneously; thus, it merely assists their strength and superiority. Among the eight consciousnesses, this consciousness alone is the strongest in being able to move the body and initiate speech.
Its capacity to create karma of good and evil is likewise strongest. Regarding "projecting" (*ākṣepa*), it is that which can project the various consciousnesses to perform karma.
Regarding "fulfilling" (*paripūraṇa*), it is that which can fulfill the ripening fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*). Therefore, one karma projects one fruit, while multiple karmas [fulfill it].

It is capable of fulfilling the karmic forces one has created. Those karmic forces that bring about retribution in a future life draw forth the eight consciousnesses to undergo the suffering of birth and death.
Thus, the *Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses* states: "The realms and stages arise from the power of other karma.

Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* does not establish seven consciousnesses, but speaks only of the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*). From this, it is sufficient to know these consciousnesses.
The afflictions are most grave.
Having initiated the first thought on the Stage of Joy, the innate [afflictions] still manifest as entanglements and latent tendencies;
from the Far-Reaching Stage onward, they are purely outflow-free, observing with perfect clarity and illuminating the great chiliocosm.
This verse describes the transformation of the six consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

Because the sixth consciousness follows the current of birth and death, it possesses both the conceptual and innate dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). If one turns against that current and returns to the source, one likewise relies upon this very consciousness to cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Now, as the consciousness is transformed into wisdom, one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) from the stage of preparatory practice (*prayoga-mārga*).

It is only upon reaching the stage of the seventh faith that the discriminating grasping at a self is finally shattered. Tiantai says: "In this respect, it is equal [to the Śrāvaka path] in that both eliminate the four abodes of affliction (*catur-vāsabhūmi*).

From the eighth faith onward, one practices the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmāśūnyatā-darśana*) and passes through the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) until the initial mind of the first bhūmi.
Only then is the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) severed; hence it is said, "one initiates the stage of joy at the first resolve.

Only then do the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*) manifest; hence it is said, "the active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). "Entanglements" refers to active manifestations, while "latent tendencies" refers to seeds.

Since the two types of innate grasping—of self and phenomena—are what are grasped by the seventh consciousness, and the seventh consciousness lacks the power to sever delusions, it must also rely upon the sixth consciousness.

Upon entering the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), at first there is much contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) and little contemplation without signs (*animitta-bhāvanā*).

Reaching the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi, the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) constantly abide in the contemplation of the dual emptiness, whereby one finally destroys the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*). The innate grasping at phenomena (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*) is forever suppressed and does not arise;
it is only upon reaching this point that the six consciousnesses attain a state of pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) clarity, and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise the same.

It is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation. If this consciousness becomes wisdom, then within the gates of the six sense organs manifest in daily life, light will be emitted and the earth will tremble;
all actions and movements will be the great capacity and great function [of enlightenment].

The seven consciousnesses, as described in the verse, possess a nature of "substantiality-with-essence" (*saviṣaya-svabhāva*), are obscured (*nivṛta*), and pertain to both the mental faculty (*manas*) and its objects. They follow conditions, grasp at a self, and are of incorrect measure (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

These eight—along with the universal (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), wisdom (*prajñā*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*)—are associated with one another.

This verse concerns the objects, the extent, and the mental factors of the seventh consciousness. This consciousness takes only "objects with substance" (*sadravyālambana*) as its objects, because it takes mind as its object;

this is called a "true object with substance. The phrase "pervading both the phenomenal and the fundamental" (*tong qing ben*) is used to distinguish it from the six consciousnesses, which take external objects and thus have "semblance objects with substance" (*sadrūpyālambana*).
Because this seventh consciousness takes the internal seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) as the self, [it takes] the intermediate image-part (*nimittabhāga*); [thus] consciousness and...

The essential nature of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) arises through mutual interpenetration; therefore, it is called "true. Among the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), it is exclusively obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This means that although this consciousness lacks goodness or evil, it arises in association with the four afflictions and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

It obscures the true nature; therefore, it is called "obscured-indeterminate" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). The phrase "measuring according to conditions" (*pramāṇa-anuvartana*) serves to exclude [valid] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If one were to say that its object is a "concrete-essence" (*sanimitta*), then it would belong to the objective domain of inference (*anumāna*).

However, because this consciousness grasps the internal aspect of seeing as a self—taking what is not-self to be a self through constant erroneous attachment—it is called "non-measurement" (*apramāṇa*). This consciousness is exclusively...

It possesses eighteen mental factors (*caitta*). Although it lacks wholesome or unwholesome factors, because it is a defiled manas, it possesses the eight universal factors (*mahābhūmika*) as well as discernment (*prajñā*) from among the object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣabhūmika*).
This discernment is precisely the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Greed, delusion, views, and pride are all identical to this view of self. As for the remaining factors not being present:
wholesome factors are pure phenomena, whereas this consciousness is defiled; the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) are coarse and violent, whereas this [consciousness] is subtle.
Consciousness is subtle; because it functions through discernment and certainty, there is no room for doubt to arise. Because it is characterized by attachment to a self, hatred cannot arise.

Thus, there are only four afflictions. Furthermore, the four object-specific mental factors are absent: since desire involves aspiration, and this consciousness operates spontaneously without any aspiration, there is no desire.
As for resolve, it involves the confirmation of an uncertain object, whereas this consciousness always takes a determined object as its focal point.

Because it concerns present objects, there is no *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction). *Smṛti* (mindfulness) is the recollection of things previously experienced; this consciousness constantly takes as its object the present realm of experience and thus has nothing to recollect.
Regarding the absence of the four [mental factors] not fixed [to a specific category]: *kaukṛtya* (regret) is the regretting of what was done previously;

since this consciousness constantly takes present objects as its domain, there is no *kaukṛtya*. *Middha* (sleep) necessarily depends upon the heaviness and dullness of body and mind, along with external conditions.
This consciousness is of a single type and internally grasping; it does not depend on external conditions and therefore lacks sleep.

The two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra involve coarse and subtle verbalization and shallow or deep deliberation; since this consciousness functions solely by way of the internal door and is of a single type that grasps at a self, both of these are absent.
"Constantly and critically deliberating, it follows the aspect of self; sentient beings are perpetually deluded day and night.
The four afflictions and eight major [afflictions] arise in conjunction; the six evolving consciousnesses are called the basis for defilement and purity.

This verse describes the functional power of the seventh consciousness. This consciousness constantly and continuously reflects upon and measures the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

For the sake of the "self," it is said that the aspect of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) constantly and thoroughly deliberates and follows along. Regarding "constant" (*nitya*) and "thorough" (*nipuṇa*), there is a fourfold classification among the eight consciousnesses:
1. The eighth consciousness is constant but not thorough; it does not grasp a self, as it is uninterrupted. 2.
The sixth consciousness is thorough but not constant; it grasps a self, as it is intermittent. 3. The first five consciousnesses are neither constant nor thorough; they do not grasp a self.
Therefore, only the seventh consciousness is both constant and discerning, because its grasping at a self is uninterrupted.

Sentient beings remain unaware throughout the long night of birth and death due to this [seventh consciousness], as it arises in association with the four afflictions and the eight major [afflictions].
As for the sixth [consciousness] relying on this [seventh] as the basis for defilement and purity, it is because this consciousness grasps at a self in every moment, thereby causing the sixth...

The consciousness (manovijñāna) becomes defiled moment by moment; yet this consciousness constantly contemplates non-self from moment to moment, causing the six consciousnesses to become pure moment by moment.
Therefore, the six consciousnesses take this [manas] as their basis for both defilement and purity; it is thus the root of the mental consciousness.
Since this consciousness is the very foundation of birth and death, those who practice Chan meditation must first resolve to sever the four delusions and remain inwardly detached.
My vision corresponds only slightly [to the truth].
The state of equality at the initial moment of supreme joy, And the effortless practice—I constantly suppress these.
The Tathāgata manifests as the Enjoyment Body for others, Appearing as the object of experience for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

This verse explains how the seven consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom. Regarding the two types of grasping at self and phenomena—both the discriminative and the innate—the sixth and seventh consciousnesses each have their respective objects of grasping.

As for the discriminative grasping at the two [self and phenomena], from the initial generation of the bodhicitta, one cultivates the contemplation of the emptiness of persons within the six consciousnesses until reaching the stage of the seventh faith, where the discriminative grasping at the self is severed.
Thereafter, one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena and passes through the three stages of the virtuous ones (*śaikṣa*).
Upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), this [consciousness] is severed; thus, the seventh consciousness shall transform into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
Because the two types of innate grasping (*svabhāvagrāha*) have not yet been purified, this consciousness has not yet attained pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) clarity. Therefore, it is said:

"At the initial moment of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā*), the Wisdom of Equality / My effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) constantly subdues [grasping]. This means that the six consciousnesses constantly abide within the contemplation of the dual emptiness (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*).
Upon reaching the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (Far-Reaching), one finally abandons the ālayavijñāna and destroys the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).

Upon reaching the eighth stage, the Anabhoga-caryā-bhūmi (Effortless Practice), the grasping at a self is permanently suppressed, while the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) arises intermittently; therefore, it is said that [the latter] is "constantly crushed.

If these seven consciousnesses are transformed into the untainted *samatā-jñāna* (Wisdom of Equality), within the state of Buddhahood they manifest the ten kinds of perception for others (*parasaṃvedana*).
The "body" is used to preach the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; this is the capacity of the Bodhisattva.

When the practitioner’s consciousness undergoes this single transformation, the Wisdom of Immovability manifests moment after moment. The Dharma-realm becomes perfectly luminous, serene, and eternally abiding.
The eight consciousnesses are by nature exclusively non-obscured; five are universal mental factors. They arise in various realms and stages according to the power of karma.
The followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand their cause, being deluded and attached to them; because of this, they are able to engage in debate with the Master.
This verse describes the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the eight consciousnesses. This consciousness is uniquely lucid and pure; fundamentally, it is neither good nor evil.

Therefore, among the four moral natures, it is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Among the mental factors (*caitta*), it is associated only with the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*).

Because there is a subtle, continuous flow of arising and ceasing, this consciousness serves as the sovereign lord of the total retribution for the three realms, the nine stages, and the six paths of birth and death within the triple world.
Although its own essence is neither good nor evil, it is drawn forth and brought into existence by the karmic power of the other six consciousnesses.

This refers to what was stated in the verse regarding the first six consciousnesses—their capacity to attract and fulfill [karma], and their being drawn by the power of karma. It is because of this...

The consciousness is profound and subtle; the World-Honored One does not usually speak of it. Therefore, it is called the "subtle *ādāna*-consciousness. Its habitual tendencies form a torrential stream;
fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded upon it.

Previously, for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles, I spoke only of the six consciousnesses as the basis for establishing defilement and purity. Since the followers of the Two Vehicles have never heard this, they simply do not understand. Furthermore, it says:
The ādāna-vijñāna is extremely profound and subtle; the seeds of habitual tendencies form a torrential stream.

I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self. Thus it is said that [this teaching] arises from deluded attachment, for the followers of the Hīnayāna do not understand it.

Therefore, some do not believe that this consciousness exists. For this reason, the masters of the Mahāyāna cite three sūtras and four verses from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as five teachings and ten principles, to prove that this consciousness exists. Thus it is said: "Because of this, they are able to engage in debate with the Master.
The meaning of these ten proofs is explained in detail within the treatise.
Vast and boundless, the Three Piṭakas are inexhaustible; Profound and deep, the seven waves have the objective realm as their wind.
Perfumed by objects, they maintain the seeds within the root-body and the vessel-world; Departing later and arriving first, they act as the sovereign lord.
This verse describes the essence, characteristics, power, and function of the eight consciousnesses. "Vast" (hào-hào) refers to the appearance of being expansive and limitless. It means:
The nature-sea of the *ālayavijñāna* undergoes inconceivable perfuming and transformation to become the sea of karma; therefore, the substance of this consciousness is vast and boundless.

Because it possesses the threefold meaning of "store" (*ālaya*), it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. These three stores are: that which can store (*nibandhana-ālaya*), that which is stored (*ālīyante-asmin*), and... [the third store].

"I am that which is cherished and stored by attachment. This means that throughout immeasurable kalpas, the seeds and habitual tendencies of the wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions performed by the first seven consciousnesses can only be stored within this [eighth] consciousness.
Furthermore, the matured fruits and retributions produced by the first seven consciousnesses have only this eighth consciousness as their locus of storage.

Because the seventh consciousness clings to this [eighth consciousness] as the self, it is called "cherished and stored by attachment to the self" (*ātma-sneha-parigṛhīta*). — *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Treatise)

It is said: "All dharmas reside within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the consciousness likewise resides within all dharmas; they act as mutual effects and also constantly serve as mutual causes.
Through the accumulation of kalpas, cause and effect are neither lost nor destroyed; therefore, it is said they are inexhaustible.
Originally, this is the mind of profound stillness, but when stirred by the winds of objects, the waves of the seven consciousnesses arise, creating various karmas. As the Sūtra says:
The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* abides eternally; moved by the winds of objective spheres, its great waves surge within the profound abyss without ceasing for a moment.

Thus it is said that the depth is profound and the seven waves have the objective spheres as their wind. The active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the first seven consciousnesses retroactively perfume this [eighth] consciousness, because its substance possesses a stable, enduring nature that is susceptible to perfuming;
thus it is said to "receive perfuming. The seeds of the good and evil of the first seven [consciousnesses] are exclusively...

This consciousness is able to sustain [the body], and furthermore, it can sustain the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world (*bhājana-loka*), ensuring they do not disintegrate throughout the duration of a single lifetime.

Because this is its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and thus the object of perception, and because it serves as the sovereign lord of the retributive fruit for the three realms, it departs at the time of death and arrives prior to conception.
As it constitutes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of sentient beings, it is called the "sovereign lord. Its...
In truth, they do not know that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, neither born nor dying. Therefore, a sutra says: "The *ālayavijñāna* is the Tathāgatagarbha;
what is called the Tathāgatagarbha transforms into the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.
Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha possesses immeasurable, pure, and wondrous merits that accord with its nature—how could it be subject to birth and death? Now, being deluded...
As the *ālayavijñāna*, it also possesses the power and function of defiled conditions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

yet, capable of undergoing transformation in a single thought-moment, the merits of its wondrous nature are inherently and perfectly accomplished. Because truth and delusion are seen as identical in essence, these four lines of verse praise the vastness of its power and function.
"Before the Immovable Ground, one merely abandons the storehouse;
After the Vajra Path, the ripening consciousness is empty, And the Great Perfectly Pure [Mirror Wisdom] arises simultaneously, Universally illuminating the lands and atoms of the ten directions.
This verse describes the transformation into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). It means that this consciousness was previously grasped as a self by the seven consciousnesses.

Since beginningless time, [sentient beings] have continued through long kalpas, sinking and floating in birth and death. Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, practice and gradually sever habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Having passed through the three stages of worthiness (*sāraṅga*) and ascended to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) and beyond, they reach the seventh stage where they destroy the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).
Only then does this consciousness lose its name of "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Because it manifests the most grave transgressions, [it is so designated].
It is said that prior to the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one has merely abandoned the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Because subtle clinging to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) and tainted seeds of wholesome karma still arise intermittently, they continue to project subsequent fruits; thus it is called the "maturation-consciousness" (*vipāka-vijñāna*). Upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) and subsequently realizing the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the maturation-consciousness finally becomes empty.
This is what is meant by those words. When the maturation-consciousness is empty, one transcends cause and effect, and only then is it transformed.

Regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the phrase "stainless and simultaneous arising" means that within the stage of Buddhahood it is called the "Stainless Consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*).
This is pure *tathatā* (suchness), meaning the manifestation of the *dharmakāya* associated with mirror wisdom.

It is perfectly luminous and universally illumines the dust-like lands of the ten directions; therefore, it concludes by stating, "universally illumining the dust-like lands of the ten directions," because principle and wisdom are of one suchness.
Only then does one realize the ultimate essence of the single mind. This is the pinnacle of Vijñaptimātra and the supreme fruition of the Tathāgata.

Contemplate this consciousness with care; it is profoundly hidden and difficult to shatter. As long as even a hair’s breadth of this consciousness remains unpenetrated, one will ultimately remain on the shore of birth and death.
Among the ancient worthies and patriarchs, there was none who transcended the Buddhas and patriarchs without first shattering this consciousness.

Regarding this discourse: if people today have not yet forgotten the cycle of birth and death, and even a hair’s breadth of the seeds of defilement within their minds has not been purified, yet they claim to have realized the Way—how can this not be called claiming to have attained what one has not attained, and claiming to have realized what one has not realized? Is it not something to be feared?

This treatise has long possessed a traditional interpretation, yet contemporary commentators are numerous. However, by minutely analyzing names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), it becomes increasingly difficult to enter;
consequently, practitioners who have not personally received instruction turn back as if gazing at a precipice.

Even those who have long relied upon lecture halls but ceased their studies to practice *chan* (meditation) merely examine the "critical phrase" (*huatou*)—yet the arising and ceasing within their own minds persists.

As for the enumeration [of the verses], there is simply nothing that can be done. Although this treatise is said to belong to the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school, it merely reveals the characteristics of "mind-only.
If one does not understand this, it will be difficult to investigate the mind, and one will inevitably fall into the error of being satisfied with a mere fragment.

Therefore, although my commentary here does not follow the wording of the original treatise entirely, I have extracted its essential meaning and rephrased it so that students may grasp it at a single glance.
It is precisely through this that one awakens to the mind; it is not merely for the sake of discriminating between names and characteristics.

If you hold me accountable for the crime of fabricating these far-fetched doctrines, I certainly dare not decline such reproach. Yet, for those who practice cultivation, they may well not be without merit.
It is my hope that wise and enlightened gentlemen will grasp the intended meaning and set aside the literal words.
○ The Sixth Patriarch Master’s Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom:

Regarding the transformation of consciousness into wisdom as taught in the scriptures concerning the nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Sixth Patriarch teaches that the very essence of consciousness is itself wisdom; there is no further need for transformation.
It is simply that upon awakening to the self-nature purity of the eight consciousnesses, their very essence is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement that the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is "the mind being free from illness," this refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), which is defiled and ignorant; such ignorance is the illness of the mind. If there were no illness of defilement, [this wisdom would be fully manifest].
Then the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) manifests moment by moment.
As for the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), one perceives that it is not produced through effort;
the six consciousnesses are fundamentally the wisdom of wondrous observation. When responding to objects, if one were to claim this as a personal achievement, [it would be a delusion].

If one clings to the view of self, this constitutes consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one does not dwell upon the achievement of merit, then daily activities responding to conditions will be nothing other than the single, wondrous wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
The wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) is identical to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
It is said that the first five consciousnesses transform into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). However, this transformation is not necessarily required.

If one simply awakens to the pure, perfect, and luminous nature of the eight consciousnesses, then the emission of light and the shaking of the earth through the gates of the five sense organs—all such activities—are the functioning of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
"Five, eight, six, and seven: fruit and cause, transformation. It is merely the transformation of names and conventions; there is no real nature.
This statement refers to the stages of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*).

Although it is said that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform within the state of the cause, while the fifth and eighth consciousnesses transform upon the attainment of the fruit, in reality, there is nothing that transforms and nothing that is transformed. It is merely the transformation of their names; their essence does not transform.
Therefore it is said: "One merely transforms names and words; there is no real nature.
If one does not harbor attachment toward that which is transformed, then amidst the profusion of activity, one eternally abides in the *nāga-samādhi*.
This concludes the preceding meaning of transforming while not transforming. As for what is called "transforming consciousness into wisdom," there is nothing else.
This is a subtle art. However, regarding the place where thoughts flow and turn from moment to moment in daily life:

if one allows the mind to linger and become attached, wisdom becomes consciousness; if, at the place where thoughts turn from moment to moment, the mind remains unattached and does not form emotional roots, then consciousness becomes wisdom.
Thus, at all times, one constantly dwells in the great samādhi of the nāga. How could this be a mere "turning-back" turning?
Contemplating these verses of the Sixth Patriarch, which elucidate the subtlety of consciousness and wisdom, is like pouring ambrosia into a parched throat.
Through such profound contemplation, what aspect of the *lakṣaṇa* school is not the upward path of Chan meditation? I—
Formerly, while residing at Mount Wutai, I dreamed of ascending to Tuṣita Heaven, where I personally beheld Maitreya, who explained the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) to me, saying:

"Discrimination is consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-discrimination is wisdom (*jñāna*). Consciousness is based on defilement; wisdom is based on purity. Defilement entails birth and death; purity results in the various Buddhas.
Because of this, I awakened to the essential principle of Consciousness-Only. Although these were but words from a dream, they cannot be spoken to one who is still dreaming.
The General Explanation of the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses (concluded).
